title: MCP 2026-07-28 Spec: The Stateless Rewrite
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol project shipped the **2026-07-28 specification** — described by its maintainers as the largest revision in MCP's history. Its release candidate had locked on May 21, 2026 after community review through the project's Working Groups and Spec Enhancement Proposal (SEP) process. This page covers what changed and why, as a follow-up to the original MCP architecture described in [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents).

---

## The Core Change: Statelessness

Prior MCP versions required a client and server to establish and hold open a persistent session before any tool call could happen. The 2026-07-28 spec moves to a **stateless protocol core**: each request now carries all the context it needs to be understood and handled on its own, rather than depending on prior session state living on the server.

This unlocks:

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span several request/response exchanges without pinning the server connection open the whole time
- **Header-based routing** — requests can be routed by HTTP headers instead of requiring a sticky session, simplifying load balancing across server replicas
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list` and similar discovery calls can now be cached by intermediaries, cutting redundant round-trips in high-frequency agent loops

---

## Authorization Hardening

The spec formalizes stronger **OAuth and OIDC** support for server authorization, closing gaps that had made ad-hoc auth implementations a common source of MCP security bugs. It also adds **enterprise-managed auth** as a first-class connector feature, letting organizations centrally issue and revoke credentials for the MCP servers their agents connect to.

---

## Extensions Framework

Instead of growing the core spec indefinitely, 2026-07-28 introduces a **formal extensions framework** with versioned extensions shipping alongside the core protocol. The first two are:

- **Apps** — embedded UI that an MCP server can render directly inside a compatible client (e.g., a rich form or dashboard instead of plain text/JSON)
- **Tasks** — structured long-running-operation tracking, so a client can poll or subscribe to progress on work a server is doing asynchronously

Additional connector-level features shipping around the same spec cycle include **observability** hooks (structured logging/tracing for tool calls) and **private network tunnels** for reaching internal-only MCP servers without exposing them publicly.

---

## Migration Impact

Because the core transport model changed, the update is a breaking change for servers and clients built against the stateful session model. Anthropic's Claude platform (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, the API) added support for the new spec as part of its August 2026 update cycle. Server authors relying on long-lived session state (e.g., in-memory per-connection caches) need to migrate that state to be derivable per-request or externalized to a shared store.

---

## Ecosystem Scale

By August 2026, the MCP ecosystem had grown substantially since its November 2024 launch:

- **10,000+** public MCP servers running in production
- **97 million+** monthly SDK downloads
- Adoption by **OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and AWS**, each integrating MCP into their own agent stacks — extending MCP beyond an Anthropic-only standard into a cross-vendor one

---

## Why It Matters

The stateless rewrite addresses the two biggest complaints from production MCP deployments: sticky sessions made horizontal scaling of MCP servers awkward, and ad-hoc auth patterns created inconsistent security postures across the ecosystem's rapidly growing server count. The extensions framework (Apps, Tasks) also signals MCP moving beyond simple function-calling into richer, longer-running agent interactions.
